title: Service bulletin for the East Cabinet reader
public_context: A service bulletin belongs to a fictional archive's microfilm room, where operators use a reader to inspect narrow ledger film. The document is part of equipment maintenance paperwork and concerns the routine relationship between a reading machine and its stored media.
source_title: Service bulletin 6: image-edge registration on the East Cabinet reader
source_text:
The East Cabinet reader began clipping the final character from pages made on the narrow ledger film. Technician Oris Vale first suspected that the film had been cut too close to its frame marks, but a low-power inspection showed the marks intact on the reel. The image shifted only when the take-up roller warmed after several minutes of use. The reader's glass gate was level; the right idler wheel had a flat patch that pulled the film a fraction toward the casing.

Vale removed the reel and laid a paper alignment strip across the gate before touching the wheel. She marked the old screw position with removable chalk, loosened the idler mount, and turned it by one notch toward the center. On the next pass, the final character stayed within the viewing field, though a thin black edge appeared on two frames. Vale wrote that the edge was part of the frame boundary, not a second line of text. She kept the original film unchanged and made a fresh contact copy only after the alignment held through three warm-up cycles.

The bulletin directs operators to compare the first and last character on each test frame before returning a reel to the cabinet. It says not to trim the film or paint over the frame edge to improve the screen image. When the reader loses registration again, the operator should stop, record the reel number, and place a paper flag at the frame where the drift first becomes visible. The paper flag is stored beside the reel box, not threaded into the film path.

Vale tested four narrow ledger reels from the same shelf. Three stayed aligned after the adjustment; the fourth still drifted when its splice passed the roller. She labeled that reel for a separate bench inspection and did not include its images in the contact copy. Vale set its box in a shallow tray with a red tag for the next shift, clipped the bulletin beside the reader controls, and asked operators to report a clipped character with its reel number and warm-up cycle, since a fault may belong to the reader rather than the film.
